item.title: Hull City v Brighton: Premier League – live
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

24 mins: Slater hooked it into the box, with Mendy heading well wide. That’s Hull’s first chance of any kind and it did not worry Bart Verbruggen.

- Premier League updates from the 2pm GMT kick-off

- Live scores | Table | Follow on TikTok | And mail Dom

Sun 22 Nov 2026 09.25 EST

First published on Sun 22 Nov 2026 08.00 EST

Sun 22 Nov 2026 09.25 EST

First published on Sun 22 Nov 2026 08.00 EST

23 mins: Some really strong and determined play from Iroegbunam earns his team a free-kick. The referee tried to play an advantage for Hull before bringing the play back.

Is this worth a shot? Slater and Belloumi stand over it.

21 mins: Another chance for Brighton, this time Ayari picking up the headed knockdown from Rutter and scuffing his effort, which means it’s an easy save for Tzolakis.

I’ve got a horrible record of live-blogging nil-nils, by the way. Just saying …

20 mins: Brighton are starting to tick here. Their short passing, their movement, their invention … it’s all superb to watch. A fluid move ends with Costinha having a shot, but he guides it wide. That was another big chance.

18 mins: A deflection runs kindly for Gomez down the right and then Rutter gets it wrong in taking the return away from his teammate. Brighton keep the pressure on, before Costinha’s cross is held by Tzolakis.

17 mins: Ironic cheers from the home fans as their team get a free-kick. Slater bundled over. Brighton have been fairly spiky in their tackling so far, and perhaps the Hull fans felt that free-kick was overdue.

A huge save from Tzolakis! That looked goal bound. It was De Cuyper whose low cross from the left was brilliantly precise, and Gomez should probably have finished it off. The Hull keeper made himself big to deny the Paraguayan at close range.

14 mins: Both keepers have had crosses to catch and errant through-balls to collect, but we haven’t really had a shot in anger yet. Gomez drills in a powerful cross low from the right but nobody in a Brighton shirt is anywhere near it.

13 mins: Brighton are actually playing more on the counterattack at the moment, which isn’t quite what I envisaged for this match, against the low-blockers of Hull City.

Boscagli’s speculative cross does not find Rutter.

11 mins: Dunk has to be alert to snuff out a Hull chance, as the home side get themselves a long throw opportunity on the left.

9 mins: I’ve said this before but ‘duh, duh, duh, football in a library’ is one of the worst chants in our great game.

8 mins: Brighton are finally getting into it, pushing Hull back with a prolonged period of possession. The black and amber shirts are shuttling back and forth to keep the visitors chanceless, at the moment. Good disciplined defence.

6 mins: Hull’s shape does resemble more of a 4-3-3, or 4-5-1, with Cho and Belloumi being asked to get forward into wide positions and support McBurnie. The home team have started confidently.

4 mins: Rutter and Gomez link up nicely down Brighton’s inside-right channel but Tzolakis is there to catch the former’s cutback. Nice pacy start to the game, this.

3 mins: Boscagli asks for an early corner but the referee isn’t having it.

Hull then hump it long from the resulting goal-kick, with McBurnie battering his way through bodies and feeding Cho, whose shot is wild.

2 mins: Brighton’s press baiting play deep in possession might not be so successful against a Hull team who are happy to sit in a low block, even at home. But the home side have come out quite aggressively, with Regan Slater barging into Diego Gomez to concede a free-kick.

KICK OFF

A bleat of Peter Bankes’s whistle gets us off and running in Humberside.

Teams are out. Let’s do this thing.

Some important pre-match news for me personally … my significant other has brought a tube of sour cream and onion Pringles into my home office. Huge. Absolutely elite live blogging snack. Less than 10 minutes until KO now.

Fabian Hürzeler sounded a little way of Hull in his pre-match press conference, citing the Tigers’ narrow 1-0 defeat to table-topping (and possible title rivals) Arsenal as a template for how today’s game might go.

“I think they do an impressive job,” Hürzeler said. “They had a brilliant start in the Premier League. They are very structured. Against Arsenal, I think Arsenal suffered. They [Arsenal] didn’t create a lot of big chances, and therefore we need to be patient because we also know that Hull are really good in transition.

“They also have individual quality in their team. Very well structured, very well organised, good in transition, good in set pieces, and I think it’s not an easy place to go to.”

Hull obviously beat Manchester United 2-0 in their opening home game and have drawn four successive matches at the MKM Stadium since, so that proves Hürzeler’s point somewhat.

Well, maybe only City will lose this afternoon, Elisabeth Terland scored for United as I was typing.

Women’s Super League: Both Manchester clubs are in serious danger of suffering shock defeats in the early WSL games this afternoon. The two matches are approaching their denouement, so catch the latest with Emillia Hawkins on our clockwatch blog.

My personal two-pennies-worth is that Brighton will probably fall away from the title race at some stage after Christmas. Their fixture list in the short term is fairly inviting, so I see their lofty position being sustained for a little while.

But realistically, a top five finish and Champions League qualification should be their primary objective. That’s really not impossible when you consider the struggles of Manchester United and Chelsea, and the possible fate of Manchester City if and when a verdict/punishment arrives re their 115s charges.

The fact Fabian Hürzeler could achieve that just after his 34th birthday would be an astonishing feat in itself.

A reminder you can follow The Guardian’s live Premier League Golden Boot tracker here:…

item.description:

Brand beaten by Casasola for second day in a row in X20 Beringen thriller

24 hours after her first win of the season at HG Cross Lokeren, at which Lucinda Brand succumbed to Sara Casasola's superior form, the Italian national champion triumphed again on hilly Beringen course, round 3 of the X2O Badkamers Trofee.

In Beringen, Casasola picked up where she left off on Saturday, leaving Brand and everyone else behind in the opening laps. This time, though, the world champion stayed within 10 seconds of the Italian and after a flying fourth lap (of six), Brand had joined the front of the race. However, Casasola stayed glued to her rival's wheel until late in the fifth and penultimate lap when Brand went flying over her handlebars on the descent, reportedly injuring a rib in the fall. The Italian then almost doubled her advantage in the final lap to take another terrific victory and prove her stellar form just a week out from the start of the UCI World Cup.

The battle for third was the closest of the race, with Aniek van Alphen ultimately beating Fem van Empel to the final step of the podium.

item.title: Frick delivers on 'heavy metal football' promise
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Frick delivers on 'heavy metal football' promise

If "heavy metal football" is what Aberdeen did, indeed, serve up at Kilmarnock on Saturday, Dons supporters will be eager to see more of this type of concert.

New head coach Mario Frick used the phrase in the build-up to his first game in charge and his team did not disappoint.

The 4-2 Rugby Park victory was bombastic, chaotic and end-to-end - just one of six goal-laden Scottish Premiership games on Saturday.

The four Aberdeen strikes - two from Kevin Nisbet and one each from Brad Lyons and Findlay Marshall - showed Aberdeen's attackers at their best with fine finishing.

In the work in progress column, though, is defending, with the visitors lapsing badly for Killie goals scored by Greg Kiltie and Tyreece John-Jules.

All in all, it was an ideal start for former Luzern boss Frick.

'Just the beginning', says new head coach

Frick was not a complete unknown to Scottish football when he was appointed during the international break - but the reference point was somewhat obscure.

Playing for Liechtenstein at Hampden in 2010, Frick gave the visitors a shock second-half lead.

The end of that game was reminiscent of the kind of heavy metal the head coach was talking about pre-match as Stephen McManus headed Scotland's winner after Kenny Miller's leveller.

Speaking after his Premiership bow, the former Luzern boss described himself as "very happy, very proud" of his new team.

"With only three training session, you can see so many attacking patterns in that first half, which was amazing," he told BBC Scotland.

"We struggled the first few minutes with some players that hadn't played in a long long time and the 1-0 lead helped. First half was very good, the second half, complicated, because Kilmarnock played very well. We were very lucky, but at the end, I think it is a deserved victory and we are very happy."

When asked if he was happy with the players trying to show his style, Frick replied: "Yes, for sure, after two training sessions, I saw a lot of it in the first half.

"It is a good start for us, but it is just the beginning."

Former Scotland midfielder Derek Ferguson took in the match at Rugby Park and was impressed with the visitors.

"As an attacking force, I thought they were good to watch," the former Rangers player said.

"They've got a big game on Tuesday night, against Rangers, so Rangers will need to be at their best, on their toes if they're going to get a result.

"It was the perfect result, obviously, for the manager coming in.

"There was more energy, more legs, more running power. They were winning a lot of the duels.

"It's something to build on, but they've got to work on that defence. They've got to be more solid if they're going to go forward."

Next up Ibrox and a season's third meeting with Rangers.

The two previous encounters, in the Premiership and League Cup semi-final, finished 1-0 to the Ibrox side, with the winning goal coming in the second half both times.

Meetings of Aberdeen and Rangers are typically just as fraught as the Rugby Park game on Saturday.

So, more heavy metal? It probably won't be smooth jazz.

'Recovery evident' - Aberdeen fan views

We asked for your views following Aberdeen's 4-2 win over Kilmarnock.

Allan: One simple question. Why was [Ante] Palaversa nowhere to be seen under Stephen Robinson? I think the fans are due an explanation as to why both he and [Nicky] Devlin fell so far down the pecking order.

Brian: Much, much better is probably an understatement. Great entertainment and a big threat going forward and,as long as we score one more (at least) than the opposition then I will be happy. It is very noticeable that Jack Milne is much more steady when Nicky Devlin is playing. I am looking forward to the rest of this campaign.

Mike: Green shoots of recovery evident. Working as a unit from back to front has been a rarity at Aberdeen. If this is only after three training sessions, I am drooling at the mouth for what's to come. Stiff test on Tuesday, but the confidence must be there so nothing to fear.

Fred: Very positive start under the new manager. Good to see some direct attacking play but still a problem defending. An acid test coming against Rangers.

item.title: England will not get carried away by beating All Blacks
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

England will not get carried away by beating All Blacks

In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on Steve Borthwick's side's record win over New Zealand and previews the final round of Nations Championship fixtures.

If England had produced that performance two years ago against New Zealand, there would have been a lap of honour and wild celebrations.

Saturday felt like business. Job done, move on. And that is how it should be.

It was a record victory for a northern hemisphere side against the All Blacks, yet at full-time you would hardly have known it.

Even the post-match messaging from their leaders - Maro Itoje, Ellis Genge and Steve Borthwick - was that this performance had always been in them and that nobody was surprised.

However, they will want to back it up.

A tired but hurting New Zealand side will arrive at Allianz Stadium next Saturday looking for revenge.

England beat the All Blacks in back-to-back Tests in 2002 and 2003. Matching that achievement on Saturday was a significant statement.

Three consecutive wins over New Zealand, followed by a third-place finish, would leave England in a strong position heading into 2027, when the Rugby World Cup takes place in Australia.

Lose, though, and it will be a waste of some great momentum.

We have had many a false dawn with Borthwick's England, but something feels different this time.

For me, that comes down to the players taking responsibility.

Many of us ex-pros called for it during the Six Nations, and finally we are seeing the players take the lead on the style of rugby they want to play.

It is an exciting, free-flowing brand of attacking rugby that mirrors what they are used to playing in the Prem.

England's backs can compete with the very best and they tore through New Zealand on multiple occasions.

Credit also has to go to Borthwick for allowing the players to take control. That, in itself, shows how he is learning and evolving as a head coach.

Once players start getting 40, 50, 60 or 70 caps, they know more about certain aspects of the game than the coach because they are the ones out there experiencing it.

If the environment does not allow players to turn around and say 'this isn't going to work', then it is never going to work.

The reports before the Australia game suggested honest conversations took place, with the players wanting a greater say in how the team operates.

The Six Nations was probably a big turning point. The change in mood and the feel-good factor are clear in the way England are carrying themselves.

They now feel in control and, crucially, have a genuine sense of ownership in shaping the team and how it plays.

'An enormous statement about English rugby'

Lewis Moody, a former team-mate of mine, joining the team to face the New Zealand haka was an enormous statement about English rugby.

Whether you are playing in 2026 or 1926, this is England rugby. We are together.

It was a united and extraordinary moment, one that will stay with me until the day I die. There was a clear bond as Lewis embraced every England player before leaving the pitch.

That was a huge driver for England. They were able to show their emotional vulnerability before quickly switching into game mode.

A record victory over New Zealand was so fitting for the occasion, but I am not getting overly carried away by the big scoreline.

The southern hemisphere teams are coming towards the end of a brutally long season. They have done a lot of travelling and played considerably more international rugby.

New Zealand and South Africa, in particular, had the added emotion of four summer Tests against each other in the 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series.

The Springboks also looked tired and strangely out of sorts in their defeat by Ireland.

At the beginning of the tournament, we were probably looking at it thinking it was a shame that the two top teams in the world were going to be on the same side of the draw.

Now, they have both lost back-to-back games, with injuries also playing a part.

England should not get carried away, by any stretch. It will be incredibly difficult for New Zealand to pick themselves up after that defeat.

The flight is waiting to take them home, they need some rest and will want to start thinking about next year's World Cup.

England, by contrast, will be chomping at the bit. They have momentum, and everybody is itching to get the white shirt on and run out at Allianz Stadium.

Saturday will provide another really good test of how England deal with being favourites. I expect changes to be made, but I still expect England to win.

After some difficult moments during this World Cup cycle, we are now seeing proper depth start to come through.

I can name at least two quality options in every position.

Fresher France my favourites

France will probably go into the final as favourites against South Africa.

Closing out back-to-back Six Nations titles and last week's victory over the world champions has given them the confidence to believe they can secure further silverware.

The Nations Championship has been a big success in replicating tournament rugby and, crucially, teaching teams how to win tight games.

Never write off the Springboks, but France are flying high after their performances against Argentina and South Africa.

Rassie Erasmus' side have lost back-to-back games, ending any perceived sense of invincibility. However, they only needed a point to reach the final and got that in Dublin.

Now it is winner takes all, and the world champions - with back-to-back Rugby World Cups and Rugby Championships behind them - should be in their element.

Fabien Galthie has rotated his squad tremendously well, and France will have more energy heading into next Sunday's final.

Those two points gained away to New Zealand with a second-string team in July ultimately proved decisive in the final standings.…

item.title: Watford seek sixth manager in 18 months after sacking Dionisi
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Watford sack boss Dionisi after 18 games

Watford are looking for their sixth manager in 18 months after they sacked head coach Alessio Dionisi following 18 games in charge.

The 46-year-old Italian was appointed in June after the departure of Ed Still, who himself lasted only three months at Vicarage Road.

Still, Javi Gracia and Paulo Pezzolano were all also given full-time contracts after Tom Cleverley left in May 2025.

Dionisi was Watford's 12th head coach, not including interim bosses, since the end of the 2020-21 season, and leaves the Hornets searching for a 25th since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

The club have had 57 permanent managers in their 145-year history.

The decision to replace him comes after Saturday's crushing 4-0 defeat by Sheffield United at Bramall Lane.

Dionisi's dismissal caps an underwhelming start to the season, with the Hornets having won just four league games to leave them 21st in the table.

"We thank Alessio and his staff for his professionalism and their efforts," sporting director Luke Dowling told the club website., external

"As I'm sure the supporters have seen, Alessio is a really good guy and we wish him the best for the future.

"The process has started for a replacement and we hope to be in a position to announce that shortly."

Dionisi was sacked by Serie B club Empoli in March after only five months in charge following a run of five wins in 22 matches.

His spell in charge of the Hornets was his first outside his homeland and started promisingly when his youthful side beat Southampton in their opening league game.

But they won only two of their next 12 in all competitions, and despite deservedly beating Charlton on 17 October, reverses at Wolves and Norwich followed, before four points from Dionisi's final three games in charge of the Hertfordshire side and his dismissal means further upheaval for the Hornets.

Since sacking Cleverley at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, the club has now been through four permanent head coaches, as well as interim boss Charlie Daniels' two-game spell in charge.

Of those four, only Gracia, in his second spell at Vicarage Road, took charge of more than 20 games.

On the morning of their final-day drubbing by Coventry last season, chief executive Scott Duxbury wrote a statement on the club website saying Watford had made mistakes, labelling their end to the campaign "unacceptable" and "truly disappointing in the extreme".
